Source focus: 7Ca · Organs, breathing and gas exchange · Key terminology
Front: Respiration
Back: The process cells use to release energy from food. Oxygen and glucose are used; carbon dioxide and water are made.
Extra cue: Do not confuse with breathing. Breathing gets oxygen in; respiration releases energy in cells.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Key terminology
Front: Gas exchange
Back: The swap of gases in the lungs: oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out of the blood.
Extra cue: Happens in the lungs, then blood carries gases around the body.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Breathing
Back: The muscle movement that makes the lungs expand and contract.
Extra cue: Breathing is the movement; ventilation is the movement of air.

Source focus: 7Ca · Organs, breathing and gas exchange · Key terminology
Front: Ventilation
Back: Air moving into and out of the lungs.
Extra cue: Inhalation + exhalation together.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Inhalation
Back: Breathing in.
Extra cue: Diaphragm contracts and moves down; rib muscles help increase chest volume.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Exhalation
Back: Breathing out.
Extra cue: Chest volume decreases; air is forced out.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Diaphragm
Back: A sheet of muscle below the lungs that helps change the volume of the chest.
Extra cue: Contracts and moves down during inhalation.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Intercostal muscles
Back: Muscles between the ribs that move the rib cage during breathing.
Extra cue: Used with the diaphragm.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Key terminology
Front: Oxygen
Back: Gas needed for respiration.
Extra cue: Carried mainly by red blood cells.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Key terminology
Front: Carbon dioxide
Back: Waste gas made by respiration.
Extra cue: Removed from blood at the lungs and exhaled.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Key terminology
Front: Circulatory system
Back: The heart, blood and blood vessels that transport materials around the body.
Extra cue: Carries oxygen, nutrients and waste products.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Key terminology
Front: Heart
Back: The organ that pumps blood around the body.
Extra cue: Pulse is caused by the heart pumping blood into arteries.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Key terminology
Front: Artery
Back: Blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
Extra cue: Usually has thick walls and a pulse.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Key terminology
Front: Vein
Back: Blood vessel that carries blood back towards the heart.
Extra cue: Returns blood to the heart.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Key terminology
Front: Capillary
Back: Tiny, thin-walled blood vessel where substances move between blood and body cells.
Extra cue: Thin walls help exchange oxygen, nutrients and carbon dioxide.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Key terminology
Front: Plasma
Back: Liquid part of the blood.
Extra cue: Carries dissolved nutrients and other substances.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Key terminology
Front: Red blood cell
Back: Blood cell that carries oxygen using haemoglobin.
Extra cue: Adapted by having large surface area and no nucleus.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Key terminology
Front: White blood cell
Back: Blood cell that helps fight micro-organisms.
Extra cue: Part of body defence.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Key terminology
Front: Bone marrow
Back: Tissue inside some bones where blood cells are made.
Extra cue: Links skeleton to blood production.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Key terminology
Front: Skeleton
Back: The framework of bones that supports and protects the body and helps movement.
Extra cue: Functions: support, protection, movement.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Key terminology
Front: Skull
Back: Bones that protect the brain.
Extra cue: Example of protection by skeleton.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Key terminology
Front: Ribs/sternum
Back: Bones that protect the lungs and heart.
Extra cue: Another protection example.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Key terminology
Front: Vertebrae/backbone
Back: Small bones forming the spine.
Extra cue: Support the body and protect the spinal cord.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Key terminology
Front: Joint
Back: Place where two or more bones meet.
Extra cue: Can be fixed or flexible.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Key terminology
Front: Fixed joint
Back: Joint where bones meet but do not move much.
Extra cue: Example: skull joints.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Flexible joint
Back: Joint that can be moved by muscles.
Extra cue: Example: elbow.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Key terminology
Front: Hinge joint
Back: Joint that allows back-and-forth movement in one direction.
Extra cue: Example: elbow/knee.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Key terminology
Front: Cartilage
Back: Smooth, slippery tissue at bone ends that reduces rubbing.
Extra cue: Helps joints move smoothly.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Key terminology
Front: Ligament
Back: Tissue that connects bone to bone.
Extra cue: Different from tendon.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Tendon
Back: Tissue that connects muscle to bone.
Extra cue: Allows muscle pull to move bone.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Muscle
Back: Tissue/organ that can contract and relax to create movement.
Extra cue: Muscles pull; they do not push.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Contract
Back: Get shorter and thicker.
Extra cue: Contracting muscles pull bones.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Relax
Back: Stop pulling strongly; can be stretched longer by the opposite muscle or load.
Extra cue: Muscles pull; they do not actively push themselves longer.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Antagonistic pair
Back: Two muscles that move a bone in opposite directions.
Extra cue: One contracts while the other relaxes.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Biceps and triceps
Back: Arm muscle pair that bends and straightens the elbow.
Extra cue: Biceps contracts to bend; triceps contracts to straighten.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Impulse
Back: Electrical signal in the nervous system.
Extra cue: Carries messages from brain/spinal cord to muscles.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Key terminology
Front: Nervous system
Back: Brain, spinal cord and nerves.
Extra cue: Controls muscle action and reaction time.

Source focus: 7Ce · Drugs and their effects · Key terminology
Front: Drug
Back: Substance that affects how the body works.
Extra cue: Medicines are useful drugs; recreational drugs can be harmful.

Source focus: 7Ce · Drugs and their effects · Key terminology
Front: Stimulant
Back: Drug that speeds up nervous system messages.
Extra cue: Example: caffeine.

Source focus: 7Ce · Drugs and their effects · Key terminology
Front: Depressant
Back: Drug that slows down nervous system messages.
Extra cue: Example: alcohol.

Source focus: 7Ce · Drugs and their effects · Key terminology
Front: Reaction time
Back: Time taken to respond to something.
Extra cue: Can be changed by drugs.

Source focus: 7Ce · Drugs and their effects · Key terminology
Front: Side-effect
Back: Unwanted or harmful effect of a drug.
Extra cue: Important in drug safety/testing.

Source focus: 7Ca · Organs, breathing and gas exchange · Equation recall
Front: Complete the word equation for respiration.
Back: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy released
Extra cue: This is the main biology equation to memorise. It happens in cells, not just in the lungs.

Source focus: 7Ca · Organs, breathing and gas exchange · Equation recall
Front: State how to calculate breathing rate.
Back: breathing rate = number of breaths per minute
Extra cue: Count one inhale + one exhale as one breath.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Equation recall
Front: State how to calculate pulse rate.
Back: pulse rate = number of heart beats per minute
Extra cue: Measured where an artery is close to the skin, such as the wrist or neck.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Equation recall
Front: Describe the direction of gas exchange in the lungs.
Back: oxygen: air in lungs -> blood; carbon dioxide: blood -> air in lungs
Extra cue: Use arrows to describe movement clearly.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Equation recall
Front: State the relationship between pressure, force and area.
Back: pressure = force / area
Extra cue: Useful extension from the skeleton topic: the same force over a smaller area gives greater pressure.

Source focus: 7Ca · Organs, breathing and gas exchange · Progression Check recall
Front: Describe the difference between breathing and respiration?
Back: Breathing moves air in/out of the lungs; respiration releases energy in cells.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Progression Check recall
Front: Explain why muscles need oxygen and nutrients.
Back: For respiration, which releases energy for muscle contraction.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Progression Check recall
Front: Explain are antagonistic pairs needed?
Back: A muscle can pull but cannot push, so another muscle is needed to pull the bone back.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Progression Check recall
Front: What do red blood cells, white blood cells and plasma do?
Back: Red blood cells carry oxygen; white blood cells fight micro-organisms; plasma carries dissolved substances.

Source focus: 7Fa · Hazards, acids and indicators · Key terminology
Front: Hazard
Back: Something that could cause harm.
Extra cue: Example: corrosive acid.

Source focus: 7Fa · Hazards, acids and indicators · Key terminology
Front: Risk
Back: The chance that a hazard will actually cause harm.
Extra cue: Risk can be lowered with precautions.

Source focus: 7Fa · Hazards, acids and indicators · Key terminology
Front: Precaution
Back: Action taken to reduce risk.
Extra cue: Example: wear eye protection.

Source focus: 7Fa · Hazards, acids and indicators · Key terminology
Front: Corrosive
Back: Able to damage or destroy materials and living tissue.
Extra cue: Most concentrated acids can be corrosive.

Source focus: 7Fa · Hazards, acids and indicators · Key terminology
Front: Irritant
Back: Causes soreness or stinging, especially to skin or eyes.
Extra cue: Many dilute acids are irritants.

Source focus: 7Fa · Hazards, acids and indicators · Key terminology
Front: Toxic
Back: Poisonous.
Extra cue: Avoid contact and ingestion.

Source focus: 7Fa · Hazards, acids and indicators · Key terminology
Front: Flammable
Back: Catches fire easily.
Extra cue: Keep away from flames.

Source focus: 7Fa · Hazards, acids and indicators · Key terminology
Front: Explosive
Back: Reacts very quickly, releasing energy, gas and sound.
Extra cue: Can be triggered by heat.

Source focus: 7Fc · The pH scale and measuring pH · Key terminology
Front: Acid
Back: Solution with pH less than 7; turns blue litmus red.
Extra cue: Lower pH means more acidic.

Source focus: 7Fc · The pH scale and measuring pH · Key terminology
Front: Alkali
Back: Solution with pH more than 7; turns red litmus blue.
Extra cue: Higher pH means more alkaline.

Source focus: 7Fd · Neutralisation reactions · Key terminology
Front: Base
Back: Substance that neutralises an acid to form salt and water.
Extra cue: Can be soluble or insoluble. A soluble base is an alkali.

Source focus: 7Fe · Bases, salts and everyday reactions · Key terminology
Front: Soluble
Back: Able to dissolve in a liquid.
Extra cue: Soluble base = alkali.

Source focus: 7Fe · Bases, salts and everyday reactions · Key terminology
Front: Insoluble
Back: Unable to dissolve in a liquid.
Extra cue: Some bases are insoluble.

Source focus: 7Fa · Hazards, acids and indicators · Key terminology
Front: Concentrated
Back: Contains a large amount of dissolved substance in a small amount of solvent.
Extra cue: More concentrated usually means more hazardous.

Source focus: 7Fa · Hazards, acids and indicators · Key terminology
Front: Dilute/diluted
Back: Made less concentrated by adding water.
Extra cue: Dilute acids are less hazardous than concentrated acids.

Source focus: 7Fb · Acids, alkalis and indicator tests · Key terminology
Front: Indicator
Back: Dye that changes colour in acids and alkalis.
Extra cue: Used to test unknown solutions.

Source focus: 7Fb · Acids, alkalis and indicator tests · Key terminology
Front: Litmus
Back: Indicator: red in acid, blue in alkali.
Extra cue: Use litmus for acid/alkali only: acids turn blue litmus red; alkalis turn red litmus blue.

Source focus: 7Fc · The pH scale and measuring pH · Key terminology
Front: Universal indicator
Back: Indicator that shows a range of colours for different pH values.
Extra cue: Use the colour change to estimate pH on the pH scale.

Source focus: 7Fc · The pH scale and measuring pH · Key terminology
Front: pH scale
Back: Scale from 1 to 14 showing acidity/alkalinity.
Extra cue: Acid < 7; neutral = 7; alkali > 7.

Source focus: 7Fc · The pH scale and measuring pH · Key terminology
Front: Neutral
Back: Neither acid nor alkali; pH 7.
Extra cue: Pure water is neutral.

Source focus: 7Fb · Acids, alkalis and indicator tests · Key terminology
Front: Chemical reaction
Back: Change where new substances are formed.
Extra cue: Reactants become products.

Source focus: 7Fb · Acids, alkalis and indicator tests · Key terminology
Front: Reactants
Back: Starting substances in a reaction.
Extra cue: Written on the left of a word equation.

Source focus: 7Fb · Acids, alkalis and indicator tests · Key terminology
Front: Products
Back: New substances made in a reaction.
Extra cue: Written on the right of a word equation.

Source focus: 7Fb · Acids, alkalis and indicator tests · Key terminology
Front: Word equation
Back: Equation using names of substances with an arrow from reactants to products.
Extra cue: Arrow means react to form.

Source focus: 7Fd · Neutralisation reactions · Key terminology
Front: Neutralisation
Back: Reaction where an acid reacts with an alkali/base to make salt and water only.
Extra cue: Core chemistry reaction for this unit.

Source focus: 7Fd · Neutralisation reactions · Key terminology
Front: Salt
Back: Substance made, besides water, when an acid is neutralised by a base/alkali.
Extra cue: Salt name depends on acid and metal/base used.

Source focus: 7Fd · Neutralisation reactions · Key terminology
Front: Antacid
Back: Medicine containing a base that neutralises excess stomach acid.
Extra cue: Everyday neutralisation example.

Source focus: 7Fb · Acids, alkalis and indicator tests · Key terminology
Front: Acid rain
Back: Rainwater made more acidic by air pollution.
Extra cue: Can damage plants, water systems and buildings.

Source focus: 7Fd · Neutralisation reactions · Equation recall
Front: Neutralisation with alkali
Back: acid + alkali -> salt + water
Extra cue: Learn this exactly.

Source focus: 7Fd · Neutralisation reactions · Equation recall
Front: Neutralisation with base
Back: acid + base -> salt + water
Extra cue: A base may be soluble or insoluble.

Source focus: 7Fe · Bases, salts and everyday reactions · Equation recall
Front: Hydrochloric acid salt rule
Back: hydrochloric acid -> chloride salts
Extra cue: Example: zinc oxide + hydrochloric acid -> zinc chloride + water.

Source focus: 7Fe · Bases, salts and everyday reactions · Equation recall
Front: Nitric acid salt rule
Back: nitric acid -> nitrate salts
Extra cue: Example: magnesium oxide + nitric acid -> magnesium nitrate + water.

Source focus: 7Fe · Bases, salts and everyday reactions · Equation recall
Front: Sulfuric acid salt rule
Back: sulfuric acid -> sulfate salts
Extra cue: Example: copper oxide + sulfuric acid -> copper sulfate + water.

Source focus: 7Fc · The pH scale and measuring pH · Equation recall
Front: pH classification
Back: acid: pH < 7; neutral: pH = 7; alkali: pH > 7
Extra cue: The lower the acid pH, the more acidic. The higher the alkali pH, the more alkaline.

Source focus: 7Fa · Hazards, acids and indicators · Progression Check recall
Front: Describe the difference between a hazard and a risk?
Back: A hazard can cause harm; a risk is the chance it actually causes harm.

Source focus: 7Fb · Acids, alkalis and indicator tests · Progression Check recall
Front: What colour is litmus in acid and alkali?
Back: Acid: red. Alkali: blue.

Source focus: 7Fd · Neutralisation reactions · Progression Check recall
Front: State the products of neutralisation?
Back: A salt and water.
Extra cue: Use the reaction pattern: acid + alkali/base -> salt + water.

Source focus: 7Fe · Bases, salts and everyday reactions · Progression Check recall
Front: How do you decide the second part of a salt name?
Back: It comes from the acid: hydrochloric gives chloride, nitric gives nitrate, sulfuric gives sulfate.

Source focus: 7Ja · Current, components and complete circuits · Key terminology
Front: Electricity
Back: A way of transferring energy through wires by moving charges.
Extra cue: Needs a complete circuit and a source such as a cell.

Source focus: 7Ja · Current, components and complete circuits · Key terminology
Front: Charge
Back: Tiny charged particles, such as electrons, can move around a circuit.
Extra cue: The flow of charged particles is current.

Source focus: 7Ja · Current, components and complete circuits · Key terminology
Front: Current
Back: Flow of electricity/charges around a circuit.
Extra cue: Measured in amps with an ammeter.

Source focus: 7Ja · Current, components and complete circuits · Key terminology
Front: Ampere / amp (A)
Back: Unit of current.
Extra cue: Symbol A.

Source focus: 7Jc · Series, parallel and switching · Key terminology
Front: Ammeter
Back: Instrument that measures current.
Extra cue: Connect in series.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Key terminology
Front: Voltage
Back: Measure of energy transferred by electricity; the push from the source.
Extra cue: Measured in volts with a voltmeter.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Key terminology
Front: Volt (V)
Back: Unit of voltage.
Extra cue: Symbol V.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Key terminology
Front: Voltmeter
Back: Instrument that measures voltage.
Extra cue: Connect in parallel across a component.

Source focus: 7Ja · Current, components and complete circuits · Key terminology
Front: Cell
Back: Source of electrical energy in a circuit.
Extra cue: Cells push charges around a circuit.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Key terminology
Front: Power pack
Back: School-safe low-voltage supply.
Extra cue: Acts as a source of voltage.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Key terminology
Front: Component
Back: Part of a circuit, such as a bulb, switch, resistor or motor.
Extra cue: Use correct circuit symbols.

Source focus: 7Ja · Current, components and complete circuits · Key terminology
Front: Switch
Back: Component that opens or closes a circuit.
Extra cue: Open switch = gap = no current.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Key terminology
Front: Bulb
Back: Component that transfers electrical energy to light and heat.
Extra cue: Brightness can change with current/voltage and circuit layout.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Key terminology
Front: Filament
Back: Thin wire in a bulb that glows when current flows.
Extra cue: Transfers energy as light and heat.

Source focus: 7Ja · Current, components and complete circuits · Key terminology
Front: Conductor
Back: Material that allows electricity to flow through it.
Extra cue: Metals are good conductors.

Source focus: 7Ja · Current, components and complete circuits · Key terminology
Front: Insulator
Back: Material that does not allow electricity to flow easily.
Extra cue: Plastic is a good insulator.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Key terminology
Front: Resistance
Back: How difficult it is for current to flow.
Extra cue: High resistance gives smaller current.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Key terminology
Front: Resistor
Back: Component that increases resistance and reduces current.
Extra cue: Used to control current.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Key terminology
Front: Variable resistor
Back: Resistor whose resistance can be changed.
Extra cue: Changing resistance changes current.

Source focus: 7Jc · Series, parallel and switching · Key terminology
Front: Series circuit
Back: Circuit with one loop/path.
Extra cue: Same current everywhere; one break stops all components.

Source focus: 7Jc · Series, parallel and switching · Key terminology
Front: Parallel circuit
Back: Circuit with branches.
Extra cue: Current splits at branches; components can work independently.

Source focus: 7Jc · Series, parallel and switching · Key terminology
Front: AND circuit
Back: Two switches arranged so both must be closed for the component to turn on.
Extra cue: Like switches in series.

Source focus: 7Jc · Series, parallel and switching · Key terminology
Front: OR circuit
Back: Two switches arranged so either switch can turn the component on.
Extra cue: Like switches in parallel.

Source focus: 7Ja · Current, components and complete circuits · Key terminology
Front: Static electricity
Back: Attraction or repulsion caused when materials rub and charges build up.
Extra cue: Different from current electricity in a circuit.

Source focus: 7Jb · Models for electricity · Key terminology
Front: Model
Back: A representation that helps explain something complicated.
Extra cue: Circuit models are useful but not perfect.

Source focus: 7Jc · Series, parallel and switching · Key terminology
Front: Analogy
Back: Model that compares something hard to understand with something familiar.
Extra cue: Example: central heating model for circuits.

Source focus: 7Je · Electrical safety and plugs · Key terminology
Front: Fuse
Back: Safety wire that melts if current is too high.
Extra cue: Protects against overheating/fire.

Source focus: 7Je · Electrical safety and plugs · Key terminology
Front: Fuse rating
Back: Largest current a fuse can carry without melting.
Extra cue: Use the correct fuse rating.

Source focus: 7Je · Electrical safety and plugs · Key terminology
Front: Circuit breaker
Back: Safety device that switches off current if it gets too high.
Extra cue: Can be reset.

Source focus: 7Je · Electrical safety and plugs · Key terminology
Front: Live wire
Back: Brown wire in a plug/cable; part of the circuit.
Extra cue: Dangerous if touched.

Source focus: 7Je · Electrical safety and plugs · Key terminology
Front: Neutral wire
Back: Blue wire in a plug/cable; part of the circuit.
Extra cue: Completes the circuit.

Source focus: 7Je · Electrical safety and plugs · Key terminology
Front: Earth wire
Back: Green/yellow safety wire.
Extra cue: Works with the fuse for safety.

Source focus: 7Je · Electrical safety and plugs · Key terminology
Front: Ring main
Back: House wiring arrangement using a loop of parallel circuits.
Extra cue: Protected by circuit breakers.

Source focus: 7Jc · Series, parallel and switching · Equation recall
Front: Current unit relationship
Back: current is measured in amperes (A)
Extra cue: Use an ammeter in series.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Equation recall
Front: Voltage unit relationship
Back: voltage is measured in volts (V)
Extra cue: Use a voltmeter in parallel.

Source focus: 7Jc · Series, parallel and switching · Equation recall
Front: Series current rule
Back: I is the same everywhere in a series circuit
Extra cue: If one component breaks, the whole circuit stops.

Source focus: 7Jc · Series, parallel and switching · Equation recall
Front: Parallel current rule
Back: I_total = I_branch 1 + I_branch 2 + ...
Extra cue: Current splits at branches and recombines later.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Equation recall
Front: Resistance-current relationship
Back: higher resistance -> lower current; lower resistance -> higher current
Extra cue: A resistor or thin wire increases resistance.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Equation recall
Front: Voltage-current relationship
Back: higher voltage -> higher current, if resistance stays the same
Extra cue: Biggest current: high voltage and low resistance.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Equation recall
Front: Optional extension: Ohm's law
Back: voltage = current x resistance, or V = I x R
Extra cue: Only use this if your teacher has taught it; it is a useful extension beyond the pack.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Progression Check recall
Front: How do you connect an ammeter and a voltmeter?
Back: Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel across the component.
Extra cue: Voltage is measured in volts (V) using a voltmeter connected in parallel.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Progression Check recall
Front: What happens to bulbs in series if you add more bulbs?
Back: They get dimmer because resistance increases and current becomes smaller.

Source focus: 7Jc · Series, parallel and switching · Progression Check recall
Front: What happens to bulbs in parallel if one bulb breaks?
Back: Other branches can still work.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Progression Check recall
Front: What circuit condition gives the largest current?
Back: High voltage and low resistance.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Quick Quiz style
Front: A pupil says breathing and respiration mean the same thing. Which correction is best?
Back: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration releases energy in cells.
Extra cue: Common trap: breathing is ventilation; respiration is a chemical process in cells.
Choices: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration releases energy in cells. | Breathing releases energy in cells; respiration moves air into the lungs. | Both words mean oxygen moving from the lungs into the blood. | Both words mean the heart pumping blood around the body.

Source focus: 7Cb · Circulation, pulse and blood · Quick Quiz style
Front: A blood sample carries oxygen from the lungs to the muscles. Which part of the blood carries most of that oxygen?
Back: Red blood cells.
Extra cue: Red blood cells carry most oxygen; plasma carries many dissolved substances.
Choices: Red blood cells. | Plasma. | White blood cells. | Platelets.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Quick Quiz style
Front: A vessel has thick muscular walls and carries blood away from the heart under high pressure. What type of vessel is it?
Back: Artery.
Extra cue: Away from heart = artery. Back to heart = vein.
Choices: Artery. | Vein. | Capillary. | Tendon.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Quick Quiz style
Front: Which description correctly shows gas exchange in the lungs?
Back: Oxygen moves from air spaces into blood; carbon dioxide moves from blood into air spaces.
Extra cue: Think direction: oxygen into blood; carbon dioxide out of blood.
Choices: Oxygen moves from air spaces into blood; carbon dioxide moves from blood into air spaces. | Oxygen moves from blood into air spaces; carbon dioxide moves from air spaces into blood. | Both oxygen and carbon dioxide move from blood into air spaces. | Both oxygen and carbon dioxide are made inside the air spaces.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Quick Quiz style
Front: During inhalation, which set of changes helps air enter the lungs?
Back: Diaphragm contracts and moves down; rib muscles lift the ribs.
Extra cue: Inhaling increases chest volume.
Choices: Diaphragm contracts and moves down; rib muscles lift the ribs. | Diaphragm relaxes and moves up; rib muscles lower the ribs. | Diaphragm contracts and moves up; rib muscles lower the ribs. | Diaphragm relaxes and moves down; rib muscles lift the ribs.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Quick Quiz style
Front: Which statement separates ventilation from respiration most accurately?
Back: Ventilation is air movement; respiration is energy release in cells.
Extra cue: This is a high-frequency Year 7 misconception.
Choices: Ventilation is air movement; respiration is energy release in cells. | Ventilation releases energy; respiration moves air. | Ventilation is only gas exchange in blood; respiration is only breathing out. | Ventilation and respiration are identical processes.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Quick Quiz style
Front: Which statement gives the function of the skull in the skeleton?
Back: It protects the brain.
Extra cue: Protection is one key function of the skeleton.
Choices: It protects the brain. | It pumps blood to the brain. | It makes impulses for the nervous system. | It joins muscles to bones.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Quick Quiz style
Front: Which statement gives the function of the rib cage?
Back: It helps protect the heart and lungs while still allowing breathing movements.
Extra cue: Ribs protect organs but still move during breathing.
Choices: It helps protect the heart and lungs while still allowing breathing movements. | It protects only the stomach and cannot move. | It makes blood cells and controls impulses. | It joins the upper arm bone to the shoulder.

Source focus: 7Ce · Drugs and their effects · Quick Quiz style
Front: In a moving joint, which statement describes the joint itself?
Back: A place where two or more bones meet.
Extra cue: Joint, tendon, cartilage and antagonistic pair are different ideas.
Choices: A place where two or more bones meet. | A cord that joins muscle to bone. | A smooth layer that reduces rubbing at bone ends. | A muscle pair that pulls bones in opposite directions.

Source focus: 7Cd · Muscles, movement and nervous control · Quick Quiz style
Front: Why is cartilage important at the ends of bones in a joint?
Back: It reduces friction and helps the bones move smoothly.
Extra cue: Cartilage is not a muscle or nerve.
Choices: It reduces friction and helps the bones move smoothly. | It contracts to bend the joint. | It carries oxygen to the joint. | It sends impulses from the brain.

Source focus: 7Cc · Skeleton, joints and support · Quick Quiz style
Front: A tissue holds two bones together at a joint. What is it?
Back: Ligament.
Extra cue: Ligaments join bone to bone.

Back: It reacts with iron oxide in rust to make iron sulfate, helping remove rust from the surface.
Extra cue: This is an acid + metal oxide reaction example.

Source focus: 7Fd · Neutralisation reactions · Quick Check mistake check
Front: A student gives this answer: “Diluting an acid makes it an alkali.” What is wrong?
Back: Diluting an acid makes it less concentrated and usually less acidic, but it does not turn it into an alkali.
Extra cue: The pH moves closer to 7 but stays below 7 unless a neutralisation reaction happens.

Source focus: 7Fc · The pH scale and measuring pH · Quick Check mistake check
Front: A student gives this answer: “A concentrated acid is always the same idea as a strong acid.” What is wrong?
Back: Concentrated means a lot of acid particles in a certain volume; strong acid is a different chemistry idea. In Year 7, use more acidic/less acidic when reading pH.
Extra cue: This app now avoids using strong when it only means low pH.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Quick Quiz style
Front: AND circuit: switch A is open and switch B is closed. What happens to the lamp?
Back: It stays off because the series path is still broken.
Extra cue: For AND, both switches must be closed.
Choices: It stays off because the series path is still broken. | It lights because one switch is enough in an AND circuit. | It lights because switch B is nearest the lamp. | It flashes because the current splits into two paths.

Source focus: 7Jc · Series, parallel and switching · Quick Quiz style
Front: AND circuit: switch A is closed and switch B is closed. What happens to the lamp?
Back: It lights because the whole series path is complete.
Extra cue: Two closed series switches complete the path.
Choices: It lights because the whole series path is complete. | It stays off because one switch must be open. | It stays off because current is used up by the first switch. | It lights only if a voltmeter is in series.

Source focus: 7Jc · Series, parallel and switching · Quick Quiz style
Front: OR circuit: switch A is open and switch B is closed on a separate branch. What happens to the lamp?
Back: It lights because one complete branch is enough.
Extra cue: For OR, either complete branch can work.
Choices: It lights because one complete branch is enough. | It stays off because both switches must be closed. | It stays off because open switch A blocks every branch. | It lights only if branch currents are equal.

Source focus: 7Jc · Series, parallel and switching · Quick Quiz style
Front: OR circuit: switch A is open and switch B is open. What happens to the lamp?
Back: It stays off because there is no complete branch.
Extra cue: No closed branch means no complete circuit.
Choices: It stays off because there is no complete branch. | It lights because parallel circuits always work. | It lights because current can jump across open switches. | It becomes a series circuit and glows dimly.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Key terminology
Front: Voltage division in series
Back: In a series circuit, the supply voltage is shared between components.
Extra cue: More components in series share the energy transfer.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Key terminology
Front: Voltage in parallel
Back: Components connected across the same cell in parallel get the same voltage as each other.
Extra cue: Each branch has its own path across the supply.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Quick Quiz style
Front: Two identical lamps are connected in series to a 6 V supply. What happens to the supply voltage?
Back: It is shared between the lamps.
Extra cue: In series, components share the supply voltage.
Choices: It is shared between the lamps. | Each lamp gets the full 6 V plus extra from the wires. | The first lamp uses all voltage so the second gets none. | Voltage disappears after passing through the switch.

Source focus: 7Jd · Voltage, resistance and measurements · Quick Quiz style
Front: Two branches are connected in parallel across the same cell. What voltage is across each branch?
Back: The same supply voltage is across each branch.
Extra cue: Parallel branches are connected across the same supply.
Choices: The same supply voltage is across each branch. | The first branch gets all the voltage and the second gets none. | The voltage is always half in every branch, whatever the circuit. | There is no voltage in a parallel branch.

Source focus: 7Je · Electrical safety and plugs · Quick Quiz style
Front: Why should electrical equipment not be used with wet hands?
Back: Water on skin can lower resistance and increase shock risk.
Extra cue: Wet skin conducts better than dry skin.
Choices: Water on skin can lower resistance and increase shock risk. | Water always turns copper into an insulator. | Water makes the voltage of mains electricity zero. | Water changes a series circuit into a parallel circuit.

Source focus: 7Je · Electrical safety and plugs · Quick Quiz style
Front: Why is plugging too many appliances into one socket unsafe?
Back: The current may be too large, overheating wires and causing a fire.
Extra cue: Too much current can overheat wires.
Choices: The current may be too large, overheating wires and causing a fire. | The voltage always becomes zero so appliances stop safely. | The wires become thicker and less resistant. | The fuse prevents any current from flowing at all times.

Source focus: 7Je · Electrical safety and plugs · Quick Quiz style
Front: Before changing components in a school circuit, what is the safest first action?

Extra cue: Switch off before changing the circuit.

Source focus: 7Je · Electrical safety and plugs · Quick Quiz style

Extra cue: Lower voltage usually means lower shock risk.
Choices: Cells usually provide a much lower voltage. | Cells cannot supply any current. | Cells are always connected in parallel. | Cells contain no stored energy.

Source focus: 7Je · Electrical safety and plugs · Quick Quiz style

Back: The current was too high, so the fuse broke the circuit.
Extra cue: A melted fuse is evidence of too much current.
Choices: The current was too high, so the fuse broke the circuit. | The voltage was too low, so the fuse supplied energy. | The plug became a parallel circuit automatically. | The fuse measured the current and reset itself.

Source focus: 7Je · Electrical safety and plugs · Quick Quiz style

Back: It has opened the circuit to stop the current.

Choices: It has opened the circuit to stop the current. | It has increased the current so the appliance runs faster. | It has changed voltage into resistance. | It has connected the appliance to the earth wire only.

Front: Explain are house lights usually wired in parallel rather than series?
Back: Parallel wiring lets each light have its own branch, so lights can be switched independently and one broken lamp does not turn all the others off.
Extra cue: This matches the revision pack idea that branches stay on when another branch breaks.

Extra cue: Higher resistance usually means lower current.
